implementation_notes: Java's structured control flow is complete — labelled break/continue handle multi-level loop exit — so its spaghetti is almost entirely exception-based control flow (a custom `FoundException` thrown to escape a search) and long methods whose branches end in a shared tail. Java's extra twist is that a checked exception forced on every caller turns a locally-scoped control decision into an API-wide requirement, which is the most Java-specific way to produce shotgun surgery out of a control-flow choice. Static analysis is strong here: PMD's NPath/CyclomaticComplexity rules, Checkstyle's NestedIfDepth, and SpotBugs report all three shapes.
idiom_name: exceptions as control flow; labeled break through nested loops
pitfalls: A checked exception declared on an interface method forces handling at every implementation and caller — a local control decision that became a global requirement.
`catch (Throwable)` catches control-flow exceptions thrown by unrelated libraries.
Long `if/else if/else if` chains dispatching on an enum-like discriminator are Replace Conditional with Polymorphism candidates.
